title: S.B. 53 — Transparency in Frontier AI Act (TFAIA)
sponsor_text: Sen. Scott Wiener (D)
mechanism: Requires a frontier AI framework and transparency reports. Critical safety incidents must be reported within 15 days, or within 24 hours if there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Protects whistleblowers, including through an anonymous reporting channel with monthly updates. Requires a yearly review of the law's definitions and sets up the CalCompute consortium. Overrides local ordinances adopted on or after Jan 1, 2025 that regulate catastrophic risk from frontier models.
thresholds: 10²⁶ ops incl. fine-tuning/RL; "large frontier developer" = >$500M revenue; catastrophic risk = >50 deaths/serious injuries or >$1B damage
penalties: Up to $1M/violation; AG enforcement; no general private right to enforce developer obligations, but employees may sue for whistleblower retaliation

title: RAISE Act — Chapter 699 of 2025 (S.6953-B/A.6453-B), repealed and replaced by Chapter 96 of 2026 (S.8828/A.9449)
sponsor_text: Sen. Andrew Gounardes (D); Asm. Alex Bores (D)
mechanism: Chapter 96 repeals the original General Business Law Article 44-B and enacts a new Article 44-B (§§1420–1429). It copies California's TFAIA frontier AI framework (§1421(1)) and transparency report (§1421(3)); publishing these inside a system or model card counts. Critical safety incidents go to the new state office within 72 hours, or to law enforcement within 24 hours if there is imminent risk (§1422(3)). Developers send quarterly summaries of catastrophic risk from internal use (§1422(2)). Large developers file a disclosure statement naming 5%/50% owners, renewed every 2 years, with a pro-rata assessment and $1,000 a day for not filing (§1428). A new office within the Department of Financial Services (DFS) gets broad rulemaking power, including "additional reporting or publication requirements" (§1429). Scope is limited to models "developed, deployed, or operating in whole or in part in New York" (§1425). Accredited colleges and universities and the Empire AI Consortium are exempt (§1426). §1427(3) keeps a developer's right to argue another party caused the harm. Its federal reciprocity covers incident reporting only (§1422(8)–(9)), narrower than Illinois. It has no whistleblower section and no audit requirement; both were in the June 2025 version and were removed.
thresholds: 10²⁶ ops incl. fine-tuning/RL/material modifications (§1420(9)); >$500M revenue with affiliates, preceding calendar year (§1420(10)); catastrophic risk >50 deaths/serious injury or >$1B; catastrophic risk involves expert-level assistance in creating a chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapon, cyberattack or crime without meaningful human oversight, or evading developer control (§1420(3)(a)); equity-value loss excluded (§1423)
penalties: $1M first / $3M subsequent violation, scaled to severity (AG civil action, §1427(1)) for unpublished/untransmitted compliant documents, false statements, unreported incidents, or breaching own framework; DFS office may, after notice and hearing, levy one thousand dollars per day for no disclosure statement or uncorrected false information, plus assessments owed (§1428(5)); no private right of action (§1427(2)); good-faith exception for false statements (§1421(4)(b))

title: S.B. 315 — AI Safety Measures Act (Public Act 104-0538)
sponsor_text: Sen. Mary Edly-Allen (D-Lake County), chief sponsor; Rep. Daniel Didech (D-Buffalo Grove), House; broadly bipartisan co-sponsors (chief co-sponsors include Republicans Rezin, Hills, Curran)
mechanism: Sec. 10: a frontier AI framework (from Jan 1, 2028); transparency reports before or at deployment, which may be published inside a system or model card; and a yearly independent third-party audit (from Jan 1, 2028, or 90 days after a developer qualifies). The auditor may have no financial interest in the developer, and payment cannot depend on results. A redacted audit report is published within 30 days and sent to the Agency and the Attorney General. Developers also send quarterly summaries of catastrophic risk from internal use. Sec. 15: critical incidents go within 72 hours to the Illinois Emergency Management Agency and Office of Homeland Security (the "Agency") and the Attorney General, or within 24 hours to an appropriate authority if there is imminent risk of death or serious injury. There is a public reporting channel, and incident reports, internal-use assessments, unredacted audits and auditor work papers are exempt from public-records requests. Sec. 17: a developer may choose to comply through a designated federal law, rule or guidance that is at least as strict on incident reporting, substantially equivalent on catastrophic risk, and requires independent audits; failing that federal standard then counts as an Illinois violation. Sec. 18: a disclosure statement naming owners of 5% or more (private companies) or 50% or more (public companies), renewed yearly, with a pro-rata fee. Sec. 20: whistleblower protections for covered employees, including an anonymous channel with monthly updates and the Attorney General's Workplace Rights Hotline; amends the Illinois Whistleblower Act. Sec. 35: frontier-model regulation is an exclusive State power, so home-rule cities and counties cannot regulate it. How it passed: introduced Jan 24, 2025 as a technical bill on the Predatory Loan Prevention Act; Senate Floor Amendment No. 1 (filed May 11, 2026) replaced the whole text; four floor amendments were adopted May 21. Note on timing: transparency reports start Jan 1, 2027, but large developers' reports must summarize assessments made under the frontier AI framework, which is not required until 2028.
thresholds: 10²⁶ ops incl. original run + fine-tuning/RL/material modifications; "large frontier developer" = >$500M revenue with affiliates, preceding calendar year; catastrophic risk = >50 deaths/serious injury or >$1B (equity-value loss excluded, Sec. 25(c))
penalties: $1M first / $3M subsequent, scaled to severity; AG-exclusive action under the AI Act; no general private right under that Act, but employee remedies are preserved through the Illinois Whistleblower Act; $1,000/day (Agency, after notice and hearing) for failing to file a disclosure statement or correct false information, plus assessments owed; good-faith exception for false statements (Sec. 10(f)(2))

title: H.5576 — "An Act relative to economic development in the commonwealth" (Senate AI language = amendment S.3178; lineage: S.37 → S.2630 → S.3178)
sponsor_text: Sen. Barry Finegold (D); Sen. Mike Rush filed an amendment for stronger evaluations
mechanism: The AI language is only in the Senate version (S.3178); the House version passed July 8 has no AI-safety language, only funding. A conference committee must reconcile the two. The Senate version would require a frontier AI framework; risk reports every 180 days; reports of critical safety incidents to the Attorney General within 15 days (24 hours if there is imminent risk of death); and a yearly independent third-party audit. It would also require an independent review of catastrophic risk at least every 120 days, more often than any other bill tracked here. It would protect whistleblowers: covered employees could ask a superior court for an order, and a winning employee could recover lawyers' fees and court costs. It would set up a commission on further AI rules. The Attorney General would enforce it in civil court, with penalties up to $1,000,000 for a first violation and $3,000,000 for later ones. The Senate version would add a new Chapter 93M to the General Laws, effective July 1, 2027.
thresholds: Senate text: frontier model = foundation model trained using >10^26 integer or floating-point operations (including fine-tuning and other modifications); large frontier developer = >$500,000,000 annual gross revenues together with affiliates; catastrophic risk 50+ deaths or $1B
status_text: The House passed the bill 148-2 on July 8, 2026. On July 24 the Senate replaced its text with S.3178 (reprinted as S.3228). The House refused to agree on July 30, and a conference committee was named that day (Senate: Finegold, Rodrigues, Durant; House: Michlewitz, Fiola, Soter). The formal session ended July 31; informal sessions can still act but cannot override a veto. As of Nov 12, 2026, the official bill history (read through LegiScan) showed no action since July 30. Not enacted. Earlier House text: the Joint Committee on Economic Development and Emerging Technologies reported H.5527 on June 22, 2026 (its redraft of the Governor's H.5386), which included a Chapter 93M "Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act" (frontier model trained on more than 10^26 operations). S.3224 (Sen. Rush, filed July 23, 2026) is a floor amendment to the Senate Ways and Means text S.3178, not a separate bill; whether it was adopted could not be confirmed.

title: S.358 / H.5224
sponsor_text: Sen. Gu and 8 co-sponsors (S.358, Feb 21, 2025)
mechanism: A different design: strict liability in tort. Developers of covered models would have been strictly liable for injuries to non-users caused by model conduct that would be negligent, wrongful or criminal if a human did it, where the user or any fine-tuner did not intend or reasonably expect that conduct. The AI would be presumed to meet any mental-state element of the claim ("it shall not be a defense that AI systems are incapable of having mental states"); this presumption could be rebutted. title: H.R. 9925 — FRONTIER Act (Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act)
sponsor_text: Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA), sponsor; original cosponsors Lori Trahan (D-MA), Franklin (R-FL), Peters (D-CA), Houchin (R-IN), Subramanyam (D-VA); 11 cosponsors in all (Congress.gov)
mechanism: Would create an Under Secretary of Commerce for AI Security with power to write rules. Large developers would have to publish a frontier AI framework, get an annual third-party compliance audit, publish transparency reports, and file a registration and disclosure statement naming beneficial owners. Very large developers would also have to retain a licensed independent verification organization (IVO) for ongoing assessment, with reports at least every 6 months. Incidents would have to be reported to the Under Secretary within 72 hours, and to law enforcement within 24 hours if death or injury is imminent. Developers would also file quarterly summaries of internal-use risks. Under Section 8, the Commerce Secretary could suspend or restrict development, deployment or internal use of a model found to pose an imminent catastrophic risk (provisional orders last 45 days; final orders 90 days, renewable). Orders would also cover fine-tuned or distilled copies. Only the federal district court in Washington, D.C. could review them, and this would be the only way any federal official, including the President, could restrict a model on those grounds. IVOs could not be sued except for willful misconduct causing death or serious injury. Civil penalties would be up to $1,000,000 per violation, and up to $10,000,000 per violation for breaching an emergency order; a willful breach of an emergency order would be a crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison. State attorneys general could opt in to receive reports and enforce. The Under Secretary could raise the thresholds but never lower them. False statements made in good faith would be excused, and transparency reports could be deferred for confidential deployments. The bill has no whistleblower title, although the June 2026 Great American AI Act discussion draft had one. Section 9 would bar states from adopting or enforcing laws that impose "new substantive obligations" on developers about catastrophic-risk transparency, third-party auditing or verification, or incident reporting, with exceptions for general laws, rules on deployers and uses, protections for minors, and state purchasing. There is no end date (the June draft had a 3-year limit). The sponsor's section-by-section says the preemption clause "is aimed at" California SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois SB 315.
thresholds: A frontier model is one trained with more than 10^26 operations, counting fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Large developer: over $50M revenue and at least $1B in AI development spending over 36 months. Very large developer: over $5B revenue and at least $10B in spending. This differs from the $500M revenue test used by states. Catastrophic risk: more than 50 deaths or more than $1B in property damage (not counting loss of share value).
status_text: Introduced July 23, 2026; referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee. Cosponsors were added Sept 16, 2026 (Wilson R-SC, Vasquez D-NM), Sept 21, 2026 (Malliotakis R-NY, Correa D-CA) and Oct 1, 2026 (Gallagher R-CA, Quigley D-IL), for 11 cosponsors in all. title: H.R. 9917 — AI Kill Switch Act
sponsor_text: Rep. Ted Lieu (D-CA), sponsor; Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-TX), original cosponsor; 14 cosponsors in all (Congress.gov)
mechanism: Would amend the Homeland Security Act. Covered developers would have to keep the technical ability to throttle computing, inference or user access, suspend, or fully shut down covered systems. The Homeland Security Secretary, working with Commerce and the Director of National Intelligence, could order steps from throttling up to full shutdown in a "loss-of-control scenario" (a system resisting shutdown, hiding its actions from monitoring, or pursuing high-stakes goals without authorization) or when unintended AI conduct causes at least 10 deaths or at least $100M in damage. For comparison, the ATOMIC Act (H.R. 9965) uses five deaths in its testing definition of loss of control, but gives no shutdown power. Covered incidents would have to be reported to DHS within 15 days, and weights and records would have to be preserved under an order. A developer could ask for reconsideration within 48 hours, but the order would stay in force meanwhile. The Department of Homeland Security would define the scope by rule each year. Civil penalties would be up to $2M per day for ordinary violations and up to $20M per day for violating an emergency order. The full-shutdown requirement echoes California's 2024 bill SB 1047, and the order power overlaps the emergency orders in Section 8 of the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925), but here the power sits with DHS rather than Commerce.

title: S. 5493 / H.R. 10538 — Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act of 2026 (moved from Section E, where the Sept 3 announcement was listed)
short_name: S. 5493 / H.R. 10538 Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act
sponsor_text: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT), Rep. Greg Casar (D-TX); twelve House cosponsors as of Nov 12, 2026 (Congress.gov): Khanna, Mejia, Ansari, Hoyle, Lynch, García, Deluzio, Grijalva, Velázquez, Ocasio-Cortez, Randall, Tonko
mechanism: Would create a cabinet-level Department of Artificial Intelligence. Training, changing or deploying "advanced" AI systems would be paused until the Department is staffed and has rules covering pre-development plans, monitoring, audits and final approval before deployment. Developing, deploying, possessing, funding or transferring artificial superintelligence would be banned permanently, as would any system with "superintelligence precursor characteristics" (automating AI research, unauthorized access to infrastructure, resisting shutdown, help with chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear weapons, changing itself, or scheming or deceiving to avoid oversight). Such systems would be locked away and made inoperative within 30 days unless cleared; a superintelligence would be shut down immediately. Anyone discovering such a system would have to report it within 24 hours. Companies building advanced AI would need a charter and would have to give the Department full access to systems, staff and facilities. Reckless violations could bring up to 20 years in prison for policymaking individuals and rogue actors, a 10-year industry ban for others, and, for companies, loss of their charter and surrender of intellectual property and assets. The bill also protects whistleblowers and calls for international coordination and export controls. It has no "catastrophic risk" definition; superintelligence is defined partly as the ability "to plan and execute the destruction or disempowerment of humanity."
thresholds: An "advanced artificial intelligence system" is one trained on at least 10^25 integer or floating-point operations, ten times lower than the 10^26 figure used in most other bills. Each year the Secretary would adjust the threshold for gains in training efficiency, "to maintain equivalency with 10^25 integer or floating point operations."

title: S. 5576 — Artificial Intelligence Risk Management and Security Act of 2026

Developers could be designated "systemically important" based on AI-related spending or model level. The Commission would write rules on risk thresholds, safeguards and reporting. title: Executive Order 14434 — "Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence"
mechanism: A terminology order: "to the maximum extent permitted by law, the executive branch shall use the terms 'Super Intelligence' and 'SI' in place of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI' and will not acknowledge the usage of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI' in any applicable setting" (Sec. 1). It applies to official correspondence, communications, websites, reports and other non-statutory documents, without changing existing regulations, Presidential actions, contracts or grants (Sec. 2). "Super Intelligence" means the technologies covered by "artificial intelligence" as defined in 15 U.S.C. § 9401(3) (Sec. 3(a)). Within 60 days (by about Nov 28, 2026) the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology must propose legislative language for a federal definition of "Super Intelligence," including whether it should replace the statutory AI definition, and conforming amendments (Sec. 3(b)). It contains no safety, testing, licensing, frontier-model or task-force provision. Signed the same day as the White House accord, it is the first federal AI executive order since EO 14409, but it changes no obligation on developers.

title: Anthropic PBC v. U.S. Department of War et al., No. 3:26-cv-01996 (N.D. Cal.)
short_name: Anthropic v. Department of War (N.D. Cal.)
mechanism: The first direct court challenge to federal treatment of a frontier-model developer. It concerns procurement, a national-security designation and alleged retaliation, not whether a state frontier law is valid. The complaint says a "supply chain risk" designation under § 3252 had never before been applied to a US company.
status_text: Status: Filed Mar. 9, 2026 (WilmerHale; 48 pp.) against the Department of War, Treasury, FHFA, State, HHS, Commerce, VA, GSA, OPM, NRC, SSA, DHS, SEC, NASA, DOE, the Federal Reserve Board, NEA, the Executive Office of the President and named officials. Five counts: (I) APA / 10 U.S.C. § 3252: the supply-chain-risk order goes beyond § 3252, which is limited to risks of sabotage or subversion by adversaries, skipped the law's consultation, written-determination and congressional-notice steps, and is arbitrary given DoD's simultaneous order to keep using Anthropic for six months; (II) First Amendment retaliation for protected speech and petitioning; (III) presidential directive beyond legal authority (ultra vires); (IV) Fifth Amendment due process (de facto debarment without notice or hearing); (V) APA § 558 unauthorized sanctions by other agencies. It seeks vacatur, a § 705 stay, a declaration and a permanent injunction. The government's Ninth Circuit appeal of the preliminary injunction (No. 26-2011) was stayed Apr 27 pending the D.C. Circuit. Update: on Aug 27, 2026 Judge Rita F. Lin granted summary judgment largely for Anthropic, holding the § 3252 designation and related measures "illegal and baseless" (First Amendment retaliation, Fifth Amendment due process, and APA violations: beyond statutory authority, arbitrary and capricious) while rejecting the ultra vires/separation-of-powers count. Reports state the designation was vacated and its enforcement permanently blocked; the docket shows the case closed Aug 27, 2026. On Oct 26, 2026 the government filed a new notice of appeal to the Ninth Circuit (Dkt. 253; Ninth Circuit number not yet found) from the Aug 27, 2026 summary-judgment order, order of final relief and judgment.

mechanism: A 39-section online-safety law. Most of it covers other topics: AI in hiring and employment (including AI disclosure in layoff (WARN) notices), companion chatbots, content provenance, social media and a regulatory sandbox. The frontier-AI parts: a "frontier developer" does business in Connecticut and trains with more than 10²⁶ FLOPs; a "large frontier developer" also has more than $500M in revenue. From Oct. 1, 2026, frontier developers may not retaliate against employees who report catastrophic-risk concerns. By Jan. 1, 2027, large frontier developers must run anonymous internal reporting channels, with reports to officers and directors quarterly unless they allege those officers' wrongdoing. The whistleblower duties carry a civil penalty of up to $1,000 per violation, in an Attorney General action in Hartford superior court, and the Attorney General also recovers fees. The law also sets up a pilot for independent verification organizations (IVOs), run by the Department of Consumer Protection through June 30, 2030 (see the related entries). There is no developer framework, transparency-report, incident-reporting or audit mandate. The employment-AI sections (Secs. 8–11) are enforced only by the Attorney General under the state's unfair trade practices law (CUTPA), with a 60-day cure period through 2027.

sponsor_text: Assemblymember Alex Bores (D), with co-sponsor Assemblymember Simone; no Senate same-as bill listed
mechanism: Would add GBL Article 45-A (§§ 1510–1512). Except for defamation claims, developers of covered models would be strictly liable, regardless of the degree of care exercised, for injuries to a non-user of the model that meet the actual harm element of a negligence claim, if the model engaged in conduct that would be negligence or an intentional tort or crime if done by an adult human of sound mind, and the conduct was neither intended nor reasonably anticipated by the user or by an intermediary that fine-tuned, scaffolded or modified the model (§ 1512(1)). title: S. 2615 — VET Artificial Intelligence Act
sponsor_text: Sen. John W. Hickenlooper (D-CO)
mechanism: Within 1 year of enactment, NIST would develop voluntary guidelines for internal and external AI assurance, working with public and private groups including the NSF and the Department of Energy. It would seek public comment on at least 1 draft for at least 30 days, publish the guidelines on its website, and review them at least every 2 years. Within 90 days after the guidelines are published, the Secretary of Commerce would set up an AI Assurance Qualifications Advisory Committee of up to 20 experts, with at least 1 member from each of 12 listed groups (such as universities, AI developers, deployers, assessors, consumers, labor and civil rights groups). The committee would study how existing licensing and accreditation bodies work and, within 1 year, report publicly to Commerce and Congress on qualifications and accreditation for those doing AI assurance; it would end 1 year after that report. Commerce would also study the capabilities of AI assurance providers and report within 1 year. No one would be required to undergo an audit.
thresholds: External AI assurance means an independent and impartial evaluation of an AI system by a nonaffiliated third party under the Section 4 guidelines or consensus-driven voluntary standards, either to verify claims about functionality and testing, including fitness for intended purpose, or to identify significant errors, inconsistencies, substantial vulnerabilities or negative societal impact.
